For your first assessment, you will form groups of four and devise a 15-min presentation. The presentation accounts for 40% of your grade, and is be delivered during our seminar on Thursday the 19th of November.
Your presentation should take for its theme an individual part of the body, for example the heart, brain or hand.
You should tackle the science, history, and literary representation of your body part.
Tell us about how this limb or organ was understood scientifically in the 19th Century, and how its function is explored imaginatively in literature.
On the historical side, you may want to think about whether any new discoveries were made about this body part in the course of the century, or what diseases could affect it and how they were treated.

On the literary side, a good place to start may be the cultural associations between certain body parts and certain emotions or personal characteristics (e.g. heart = love). Or you might want to consider changing ideals of physical beauty, how descriptions of physiognomy are used to represent a person’s inner character, or how particular bodily features become racialized and are used to denote “higher” or “lower” types. Or how, you might want to ask, do literary treatments address the absence of certain body parts, or with the disabling or disfigurement of individuals by accident, illness or violence?
You can use as many or as few texts as you think proper as long as your focus remains on the embodied experience, in the 19th Century, of one specific body part. But you are also encouraged to consider in your conclusions how your research links to real-world questions and problems with which we grapple today.
Your choice of body parts includes (but is not limited to) the following: heart, brain, lungs, liver, stomach, hand, fingers, leg, sexual organs, skin, nerves, blood, eyes, ears, nose, hair.

You will be assessed according to the sensitivity and complexity of your ideas, your attention to the subtleties of language and imagery, and your ability to bring historical and scientific information, or historical sources, into conversation with literary sources.

Respond to one of the prompts below in an essay of not more than 2000 words (excluding works cited).
Your essay must meet the following requirements: -You must include a detailed discussion of at least two of the primary texts studied on this module (this includes the texts cited in the “Case Notes” presentations).
You must not reuse material from a previous assignment, though you can use texts you referred to during your presentation.
If you wish to write on John Keats or Edgar Allan Poe, you may choose different poems or stories from those that were set for class reading.
-You must include material from at least five secondary critical sources found in the Resource List, in the University Library, on the Victorian Web, or in a database of academic journal articles (Jstor, Project Muse) -Your essay must include a cover sheet: the new version of the coversheet is on Moodle ------------------- ‘Oh heaven!—I then felt the knife rackling against the breast bone’ (Fanny Burney).

Discuss how any two texts on the module describe the experience of pain.
‘Mens sano in corpore sano’ (‘a healthy mind in a healthy body’, motto of various hospitals and medical colleges).
How do any two texts on the module conceptualize the relationship between body and mind?
‘It has of late been thought that the Convolutions of the Cerebrum expand on the accumulation of Water’ (Keats’s medical notebook).
How do any two texts on the course respond to new discoveries in anatomy, physiology or medicine?
‘A people whom Providence hath cast together into one island or country are in effect one great body politic, consisting of head and members, in imitation of the body natural… and this body never dies’ (Robert Atkyns, seventeenth-century judge).
How do any two texts on the course make use of the traditional idea of the body politic?
‘I have a passion for fine shoulders’ (Poe, ‘The Man That Was Used Up’).

How do any two texts on the course address deviancy from sexual, gender or any other norm?
‘This living hand, now warm and capable / Of earnest grasping’ (John Keats).
In what ways is the haptic (the experience of touch) important to any two texts on the course?
‘Trauma makes people feel like either some body else, or like no body.
In order to overcome trauma, you need help to get back in touch with your body, with your Self’ (Bessel van der Kolk, The Body Keeps The Score).
Explain how any two texts on the course understand, or fail to understand, the physical effects on the body of psychological trauma.
‘The judges of normality are present everywhere.
We are in the society of the teacher-judge, the doctor-judge, the educator-judge, the social worker-judge; it is on them that the universal reign of the normative is based; and each individual, wherever he may find himself, subjects to it his body, his gestures, his behaviour…’ (Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish).

Is medicine an institution for exerting social control?
Choose two texts from the course and use to argue your case..
‘As the bacillus is easily transmissible, it won’t be long before the disease goes through them like fire through a hay-rick’ (Mitchell, ‘The Bacillus Anti-Cathay’).
How do any two texts on the course depict epidemic disease, its causes and/or effects?
‘My friend and I have principles… on which our methods of managing our infirmity are founded’ (Martineau, ‘Letter to the Deaf’).
How do any two texts on the course describe the experience of disabled people living in a society designed for the able-bodied and/or neurodiverse?
‘The inspector sahib thinks you must go to the segregation camp’ (Cornelia Sorabji, ‘The Pestilence at Noonday’).
What was the importance of medicine and/or hygiene in colonial governance?
Discuss with reference to two texts.
‘The eyes roll unnaturally in the head, without any corresponding motions of the lids or brows.

The arm, particularly, performs its operations in an exceedingly stiff, awkward, jerking, and rectangular manner’ (Edgar Allan Poe, ‘Maelzel’s Chess-Player’).
How do any two texts on the course address the novelty of human prosthetics and/or automata?
‘For Victorians, the skin was a text to be read… no longer simply a wrapping, it became a substance integral to and having a creative role in the generation of the self’ (Pamela Gilbert, Victorian Skin).
How do any two texts on the course explore the importance of the body for personal identity?
‘It was not for the purpose of creating pleasure, but of mitigating pain in the severest degree, that I first began to use opium as an article of daily diet.’ (De Quincey, Confessions of an English Opium-Eater).
How is addiction portrayed in any two texts from the course?
As an alternative to a conventional essay, you are invited to produce a creative response.

Follow one of two paths, (a) or (b), and include a list of sources that you used to research your work.
Annotate each source in your list with one sentence explaining how you used it/what you used from it in your creative response (this source list is not included in the word count).
Write the diary of a Victorian person undergoing medical treatment in a hospital.
It should be treatment for a physical condition (real or imagined), not mental.
Make sure you the diary describes admission to hospital, diagnosis, treatment by surgery, drugs, or other, and finally convalescence and discharge.
Issues to potentially consider include patient consent, the clinical method, the bedside manner, medical biases of the time, and misdiagnosis.
The patient can be a historical or fictitious person, but if historical they cannot be Fanny Burney or W.E.
Henley.
N.B.
take care to date your diary, and to make sure the patient’s experience is historically accurate for the period.
Write a newspaper article or a short story, as if for a 19th century newspaper, inspired by one of the themes or texts studied on this module.

To complete this coursework, you will design the behaviour of complex programs involving the fundamental programming constructs, such as functions, operations, and file reading/writing. A template Jupyter notebook and a text file are provided to complete the tasks. Time in class can be used to troubleshoot and get feedback on your program.
The university that hired our Software Development company is very pleased with the outcome of Coursework Midpoint Review and has requested an extension. The program that you have crafted for Coursework Midpoint Review takes in scores for 4 components of student assessment in the Computer Programming module: 
1. Coursework 1: Flowchart concepts (10%) 
2. Coursework 2: Basic Programming concepts (20%) 
3. Coursework 3: Complex program implementation (30%) 
4. Test: Theoretical and practical assessment (40%)

The program uses these individual component scores to calculate an overall score out of 100 using the formula: 
Overall_score = (coursework1 * 0.10)+ (coursework2 * 0.20) + (coursework3 * 0.30) + (final_exam * 0.40)
The resulting number (should be between 0 and 100) is then used to estimate the category using the categorical marking dataset: 
No. Category Overall Mark 
1 Gold Standard 100 
2 Upper First 82, 85, 92 
3 First 72, 75, 78 
4 Upper Second 62, 65, 68 
5 Lower Second 52, 55, 58 
6 Third 42, 45, 48 
7 Condonable Fail 32, 35, 38 
8 Fail 5, 15, 25 
9 No Submission 0

From the dataset above, 
- If the overall score is equal to 100, the output should be "Gold Standard". 
- If the overall score is between 82 and 92, the output should be "Upper First". 
- If the overall score is between 72 and 78, the output should be "First ". 
- If the overall score is between 62 and 68, the output should be "Upper Second". 
- If the overall score is between 52 and 58, the output should be "Lower Second". 
- If the overall score is between 42 and 48, the output should be "Third” 
- If the overall score is between 32 and 38, the output should be "Condonable Fail". 
- If the overall score is between 5 and 25, the output should be "Fail". 
- If the overall score is 0, the output should be "No Submission".
You are asked to add the following functionality:
1.
Functions (8 points): Split and pack up your Coursework Midpoint Review code into functions.

The program must contain a main() function and at least two other functions called "calculate_overall_score()" and "determine_category()".
2.
Input expansion (8 points): Adjust your program to ask users to enter a student ID (2-digit number), name and date-of-birth (D.o.B) by sequence, before asking for the 4 component scores from Coursework Midpoint Review (Coursework1, Coursework 2, Coursework 3 and Final Exam).
D.o.B should be in ISO format YEAR-MONTH-DAY.
3.
Loop your code (8 points): Your program should use a loop to ask for the information of three students, or until the input for user ID is "end".
4.
Calculate the students' overall scores and store them for later use (2 points).
5.
Determine the students' categories and store them for later use (2 points).
6.
Calculate students' ages (8 points): According to each user's year of birth, your program should calculate the age of the student and store it for later use.

Hint: the library datetime can be used here to make your job easier.
7.
Tabulate (8 points): Display a table that summarises the input data (ascending order with user ID) using the tabulate library.
It should look like:
UID Name D.o.B Age Score Category 
    -- ----------------- ---------- --- ------- -------------- 
   13 Lieke Martens 1992-12-16 29 86.6667 Upper-First 
   02 Cristiano Ronaldo 1985-02-05 37 73.3333 First 
   24 Lucy Bronze 1991-10-28 31 50 Third

8. File writing (8 points): Save the table into a new local file named "students.txt" 
9. Make sure that you: a. Implement robust input validation for a student's ID, D.o.B., and scores. Your program should give 
a. Warning that says "The input you entered was invalid" for any input errors (6 points) 
b. Display use of appropriate data structures for storing student information (5 points) 
c. Display use of appropriate code structures for implementing the functionality (5 points) 
10. Implement a function called `round_to_category(score)` that takes a numerical score and rounds it to the nearest category. This function should (10 points): 
a. Accept a float or integer score as input. 
b. Determine the two nearest category boundaries. 
c. Round the score to the nearest category based on which boundary it's closer to. 
d. Return the rounded score and the corresponding category.

For example: 
- If the input score is 73.7, it should return (75, "First") because 73.7 is closer to 75 than to 72. 
- If the input score is 69.2, it should return (68, "Upper Second") because 69.2 is closer to 68 than to 72. 
-Your implementation should handle edge cases, such as scores exactly halfway between two categories (round up in these cases), and scores at or beyond the extremes of the scale.
UID Name D.o.B Age Raw Score Rounded Score Category 
 -- ------------ -------- ---- ---- ---- ------------ 
 13 Lieke Martens 1992-12-16 29 86.6667 85 Upper-First 
 02 Cristiano Ronaldo 1985-02-05 37 73.3333 75 First 
 24 Lucy Bronze 1991-10-28 31 50 52 Third
11.
Distinction Advanced Function: Once everything in requirements 1-10 has been completed, for a distinction grade, extend your program with one more function called advanced().
This function should: 
a.
Be a complementary main() method that, instead of taking user input, uses the provided file as input.
b.

Accepts in its argument (filename) the name of the text file to read.
c.
Read the student information record from the provided file "StudentData.txt", which contains student IDs, names, and date-of-births.
The function should then use this data as the input for the program.
d.
Runs all the other functions used and produces a text file output (requirement 8).
12.
Advanced Generalization Function (Distinction level): Implement a function called `setup_module()` that allows the user to define the assessment criteria for any module.
This function should: 
a.
Ask the user to input the module name.
b.
Ask the user how many assessment components the module has.
c.
For each component: 
- Ask for the component name (e.g., "Coursework 1", "Final Exam") 
- Ask for the component's weight as a percentage (ensure all weights sum to 100%) 
d.
Store this information in an appropriate data structure.
e.
Return the module configuration.

While fully functioning programs and its documentation that meet all the requirements are the goal of the test, the programs and the rationale for their design, implementation, testing and debugging will be assessed for efficiency, simplicity, creativity, and good style. Please read the Grading Rubric and bring any questions you may have to your tutor during the class.

Task:
In this coursework, you are required to implement the database you designed in Coursework 1. You will use DDL statements to create the database and develop the necessary data structures to fulfil its intended purpose. Your work will be assessed through both a written submission and a lab-based SQL assessment. This coursework contributes 60% of the overall module grade and is divided into two components:
Support file and Reflection Report submission worth 20% and
In Class lab-based SQL demonstration and Presentation worth 40%.

Submission Requirements (20%)
In this submission, you are required to upload two files to Moodle:
• File1– Database Implementation Code (.SQL file OR .TXT file)
• File 2 – A single PDF file containing the following:
• Contribution from both group members:
o Student 1 – contribution to the project (250–300 words) (Student Name and ID mentioned on the top of this section)
o Student 2 – contribution to the project (250–300 words) (Student Name and ID mentioned on the top of this section)
• Individual reflections from each member:
o Student 1 – individual reflection (250–300 words)
o Student 2 – individual reflection (250–300 words)
• Each reflection should address:
o What you have learned from both coursework 1 and Coursework 2
o The challenges you encountered during the database design and implementation process

To do this, you should:
1. First, modify ERD and physical data model according to feedback received for coursework1 if necessary. (NOT require submission on this)
2. Then, use SQL statement to implement database based on the revised physical data model in step1：
a. Create tables.
b. Set appropriate constraints which including column data types, primary key and foreign keys.
c. Consider if each column allows NULL value or NOT.
d. Insert meaningful values into each table (at least insert at least 5 records to each table for retrieving purpose in lab assessment).
NOTE: you can use ‘EmployeeInfo’ schema as example to prepare your SQL code that you chose for your Coursework.
In Class Demonstration and Presentation (40%)
Lab assessment will be conducted on week-13 and Week-14, the implemented database will be examined in this assessment from 3 perspectives (20%):
1.
All tables are created properly based on physical data model.
2.

Appropriate constraints are set including data types, primary and foreign keys.
3.
Meaningful sample data is populated into each table.
The understanding of SQL will be also examined in lab session in the form of (20%):
1.
Tutor makes 1 question for each student based on the content of your database SQL operations.
2.
You are expected to write SQL solutions to obtain the request results by executing the query in the given time (5 to 7minutes)
3.
The examined SQL coverage as follow:
a.
Inserting appropriate values into tables.
b.
Perform SELECT operations using:
i.
Special operators.
ii.
Comparison/mathematical operators.
iii.
Logical operators.
iv.
Aggregation functions.
v.
Ordering operations.
vi.
Grouping operations.
vii.
Joining tables (inner, outer, self, and/or left/right).
viii.
Nested queries.
c.
Defining database views.

To achieve maximum success in this task:
• Follow your revised design carefully: Ensure your database implementation strictly matches the improved physical data model from Coursework 1, including correct tables, relationships, and naming conventions.
• Set constraints accurately: Apply appropriate data types, primary keys, foreign keys, and NULL/NOT NULL rules. This is essential for demonstrating correct relational structure and for meeting the rubric’s “Excellent” category.
• Populate meaningful sample data: Insert at least five realistic and coherent records per table. This data will be used in your lab assessment queries, so make sure values make sense and reflect real-world scenarios.
• Write clean, well-structured SQL code: Use clear formatting, consistent naming, and a variety of SQL features (joins, aggregations, nested queries, grouping, views). Demonstrate beyond basic SELECT queries to achieve full marks.
• Prepare for the lab SQL demonstration: Understand your own database thoroughly, as each group member will answer one simple and one complex SQL question based on your implementation. Practice writing queries without relying on external help.
• Submit the correct files and complete reflections: Upload both required files (SQL file + PDF). Clearly describe each member’s contribution and provide thoughtful reflections (250–300 words each) on learning, challenges, and skills gained.

Overview
Students will work in groups of 3 or 4 people.
Each group will produce a ‘full stack’, dynamic web application which can be deployed using Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment techniques.
Technologies
The technologies used in the module are as follows:
Frontend:
• HTML
• CSS
• JavaScript
• PUG templating system
Backend:
• Node.js
• Express.js
• MySQL database
DevOps and CI/CD:
• Docker
• Git
• Github actions
Project management:
• Github project
Your application must be built using the tools and techniques taught in the module.

Theme
For 2026, our theme will be “Sharing, exchange and building community”.
To address the theme, students should consider how they can use their skills to help solve real and specific problems, for example: waste, climate change and cost of living crisis, and/or support and develop their interests and hobbies. They will do this by creating a dynamic, database driven web application through which users can exchange goods or services co-operatively, for mutual benefit rather than financial gain.
Each group will choose one of the project ideas presented by the staff team - indicative examples below. They can suggest their own idea which will need to be validated by a member of the staff team by the end of week 2.

Indicative project ideas
• Minimising food waste by sharing excess food
• Study buddies: peer support for students
• Ride sharing to university
• Book and record swap
• Community languages – teach and learn
• Circular fashion – re-make and mend
• Sharing outfits for job interviews, special occasions etc
• Running and cycling buddies
• Game tips and tricks
• Recipe swap
The groups will be expected to consider usability, security and ethics as they develop their application. While all groups will start with basic functionality, the projects will allow increasing creative input and unique ideas as they develop.
Deliverables
You will work on the project using a ‘scrum’ project management methodology. This means that you will work as a team to deliver your project iteratively.
Your progress will be discussed weekly during ‘stand-up ‘meetings in lab time with your lecturer, and formally via the code-review assessment points.
The following details the deliverables for each sprint:

Sprint 1: Review point: Lab of Week 4
The aim of this sprint is to check that the project workflow is set-up for the team, you have clarified your project idea and adopted a code of conduct.
Checklist Submission 1

• A single PDF document with:
 Your group members and group name
 Project description refined
 Code of Conduct
 At least two ‘Personas’

 Meeting records completed
Sprint 2: Lab of Week 6 (Career week)
The aim of this sprint is to assemble the initial requirements and ensure that specifications are ready for sprint 3.

Checklist Submission 2
The following must be in place:
• A single PDF Document with:
 Features for your application defined as user stories
 Use case diagram
 Sprint 3 specification prepared with at least: user stories, wireframes, activity diagrams.
 Other artefacts may be included such as sequence diagrams, ERD diagram, class diagram, designs, colour schemes
• A screenshot of your Kanban board

Sprint 3: Review Lab of week 10
The aim of this sprint is to begin the application development by creating some simple features. All members of the team must show that they can build the development environment and have contributed code. For your sprint review you will be expected to be able to have your database populated and be able to run your code

Checklist Submission 3
Initial requirements implemented using MySQL, Express and PUG, using Docker containers for the team development environment and demonstration. To include at minimum (these pages must use data pulled from your database):
• Users list page
• User profile page
• Listing page
• Detail page

A single PDF document with:
• The user stories you implemented in sprint 3 (Can be copied from Sprint 2 documentation)
• Database design

• A screenshot of metrics from github showing that all team members are participating

In your sprint 3 review, you will plan your final sprint which will be tailored to each groups progress

Sprint 4: To be presented in Week 13/14
The aim of this sprint is to complete your ‘MVP’ to by adding features and refining your design as much as possible. The scope of your sprint 4 will be tailored to each group and will be determined in your sprint 3 review meeting.
You will also add some CI/CD workflows using github actions.
Groups will present to the whole class in weeks 13 and 14.
Checklist Submission 4
Web application: Intermediate and/or advanced requirements implemented to include at least some of:

• Basic matching algorithm

DevOps and CI/CD

Presentation
A presentation of your application idea, ethical issues and and MVP during week 12. Ppt file to be uploaded to Moodle.

Individual Assessment
Individual contributions to the team will be assessed based on attendance at the various meetings and code reviews, and via the metrics gathered from tools such as GitHub.
Individual contributions can lead to a scaling of the overall coursework grade if the module team have evidence that illustrates a lack of contribution to the team deliverable.

▪ No attendance by any group member at the meeting will mean the code review will be marked at 0%

Individuals attendance at reviews will be monitored to ensure the team is contributing collectively to the project.

This means that you have a computer with your application ready to run and/or your documentation ready for display.

Individual component
20% of coursework
The individual reflection element of this assignment has two parts:
1. A STAR story.
2. A short reflection on your experience of the module and any lessons learned that you will apply to your Final Year Project.
Task 1: STAR Story
The STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is a commonly used way to evaluate candidates during job interviews.
It is comprised of 4 steps:
• Situation: Describe the situation and when it took place.
• Task: Explain the task and what was the goal.
• Action: Provide details about the action you took to attain this.
• Result: Conclude with the result of your action.
The STAR method is preferred by many job recruiters because it gathers information about candidates' real experiences, and what they actually did in real situations.
A STAR story is not a theoretical explanation of what you think should be done, or where you tell the interviewer what you think is the desired ‘right answer’.

We are asking you to do this to give you an opportunity to practice this method and prepare you for future interviews.
We also want to help you understand how you can use your experiences at university to illustrate your personal strengths and allow you to stand out from other candidates by telling stories about real situations.
You can find many useful examples online, for example:
https://nationalcareers.service.gov.uk/careers-advice/interview-advice/the-star-method
https://www.betterup.com/blog/star-interview-method
Your Task:
Please choose one of the following questions and answer it using the STAR method.
That means you should explicitly write a paragraph about each of the sections (i.e., describe the situation, describe the task, describe the action you took to address this task, and describe the result).
Things to remember:
• You must write about a real situation that you faced during your coursework.
• Do not use AI for this assignment.

If you hand in an answer that is generic and which your lecturer cannot recognize from the work you have done, your work will not be able to pass.
• You should not name names in your group or apportion blame.
If you need to refer to something somebody else has done, please just refer to ‘a group member’.
• You should be able to tell your STAR story from a positive perspective.
Even if things went wrong, a good STAR story can show that you took effective action to resolve a difficult situation.
The questions: Please choose one:
• Tell me about a time when there was a disagreement in your team.
• Tell me about a time when you were stuck on a task.
• Tell me about a time when your project seemed to be stuck in a rut and not moving ahead at the required pace.
• Tell me about a time you were concerned that a deadline might be missed.
• Tell me about a time when you had to correct a colleague's work.
• Tell me about a time when you had to challenge the actions of someone in your team.

• Tell me about a time when you made a wrong decision
• Tell me about a time when you had to shift priorities
Remember STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Your answer must have a well-defined short paragraph about each of these.
Task 2: Module Reflection
Please write a paragraph (do not use AI) in which you consider the main lessons learned from this module. Write about how you will use these lessons learned when you are devising your final year project.
You may wish to think about issues such as:
• Time management.
• Things that you found interesting.
• Things that you realized you were good at.
• New topics that you thought you might want to explore further.
• Aspirations you may have to create a project that could address a problem you have recognized in your everyday environment.

ASSIGNMENT STRUCTURE: This assignment comprises five interconnected tasks.
Tasks 1–4 are preparatory work and, Task 5 is the final assessed presentation that integrates all prior work.
Assessed component (60% slides + 40% Presentation).
TASK 1: SELECTION OF E-COMMERCE PLATFORM.
You will select a distinctive e-commerce application or website for detailed research on user experience.
This will form the focus of all subsequent tasks.
Step 1: Choose Your Platform: Select an e-commerce platform that interests you.
Do not select Amazon.
The following link provides a starting list of options, but you are not limited to these: https://www.tigren.com/blog/ecommerce-companies/ Step 2: Document the Platform: Gather basic information about your chosen platform: Name and description: What is it?
Who uses it?
Key features: What are 3–5 discrete, user-facing features?
User roles: Who are the primary user types (e.g.
buyer, seller, admin)?
Business model: How does it make money?

Reach: Geographic scope, user base size (if available).
TASK 2: USER EXPERIENCE RESEARCH – EXPLORE METHOD.
You will choose one Explore' UX research method and use it to document and analyse a specific feature of your chosen e-commerce platform.
Step 1: Identify and List Features: A feature is "a discrete piece of functionality desired by stakeholders." Identify 3–5 features of your chosen platform and, for each, identify which user role(s) benefit from it.
Example: Feature: Product reviews; User roles: Buyer (to inform purchase decisions), Seller (to receive feedback).
Step 2: Choose an 'Explore' Method and Conduct Research: Select one of the following UX research methods and apply it to analyse a single feature in depth: Persona: Create 1–2 detailed personas representing your target users.
Journey Mapping: Map the end-to-end user journey for a specific task involving your chosen feature.
User Story Mapping: Break down user goals into user stories and tasks.

Step 3: Conduct User Interviews: Interview at least 2 users of your chosen e-commerce platform to gather qualitative data.
These users should represent different user roles or perspectives (e.g.
a frequent buyer and a first-time user).
Topics to explore: How do they currently use the feature you are analysing?
What problems or friction points do they encounter?
What would improve their experience?
Documentation: Record key insights, direct quotes, and observations.
Step 4: Analyse and Synthesise: Use your chosen method to synthesise your interview data.
You may examine the same feature from multiple user perspectives (e.g.
both buyer and seller viewpoints).
Your chosen UX method; 1–2 key personas, user stories, or journey map; Summary of user needs and pain points (informed by interviews).
TASK 3: USABILITY TESTING.
You will conduct a ‘think-aloud' usability test’ to evaluate a feature of your chosen e-commerce platform and gather evidence for recommendations.

Step 1: Plan Your Test: Feature to test: Use the feature you identified in Task 2; Participants: Recruit 2–3 participants (can include the same users as Task 2, or new ones); Tasks to perform: Design 2–3 realistic tasks that use your chosen feature.
Step 2: Execute the Test: Use the Think-Aloud Test Template available on Moodle; Ask participants to verbalise their thoughts as they perform tasks; Observe and note difficulties, confusion, successes, and unexpected behaviour; Ask clarifying questions.
Step 3: Analyse the Data and Generate Recommendations: Identify usability issues from your observations; Categorise issues by severity (critical, major, minor); For each issue, propose concrete recommendations for improvement; Categorise recommendations as: 'Easy wins' Quick, low-cost fixes with notable benefits, 'Sound investments': More complex improvements that deliver substantial long-term value.
TASK 4: INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY, LEGAL/ETHICAL, AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS.

You will conduct critical research into the societal and environmental impacts of your chosen e-commerce platform.
1.
Key Facts: Expand on details about your case study: Number of users / user base demographics, Geographic reach, Annual revenue or funding (if public), Company ownership and structure.
2.
Intellectual Property: Examine intellectual property (IP) crucial to your case study: Software licenses, Content licenses, Trademarks and patents, Critical analysis.
3.
Legal, Ethical, and Social Issues: Identify and analyse trade-offs in the platform's design and operation: Privacy, Labour rights, Human rights, Surveillance and bias, Emerging technology issues, Trade-offs.
4.
Environmental Impacts: Consider the environmental footprint of the platform and its effects: Computational impacts, Service design impacts, Net environmental effect.
5.
Conclusion and Synthesis: Summarise your research.
What are your key findings?

Can you apply your findings to draw conclusions and/or make recommendations for your case study and perhaps more widely?
TASK 5: FINAL PRESENTATION.
You will produce a single, cohesive PowerPoint presentation that integrates Tasks 1–4 and deliver it live in class.
Presentation Structure (Suggested): 1.
Recommended slide breakdown (total ~10–12 content slides); 2.
Title Slide (Student name, student ID, module code, submission date); 3.
Platform Overview (1 slide); 4.
UX Research Method & Findings (2–3 slides); 5.
Usability Testing (2–3 slides); 6.
Intellectual Property Analysis (1 slide); 7.
Legal, Ethical, and Social Analysis (2 slides); 8.
Environmental Impacts (1 slide); 9.
Conclusions and Recommendations (1 slide); 10.
References Slide (1 slide).

Design and Professional Quality Standards: -Font size: Minimum 18pt for body text; 28pt+ for headings - Readability: Use high contrast between text and background; avoid walls of text - Visuals: Include screenshots of the platform, personas, journey maps, process diagrams, and data visualisations (if applicable) - Consistency: Use a coherent colour scheme and font family throughout - Citations: Each claim should be backed by an inline citation (e.g. "[1]" placed after the claim) with a corresponding numbered reference on the references slide

Use IEEE referencing format (numbered citations in brackets [1], [2], etc., with a numbered reference list at the end). All claims must be supported by credible sources: Academic journals (via Springer Link, Google Scholar, etc.), Industry reports and case studies, News articles and investigative journalism, Company transparency reports or official statements, Government or regulatory documents. Referencing should be done following IEEE style. Information can be found at the library web site.

Assessment Requirements Data Visualisation Assessment Brief (CMP020L013) The summative assessment for this module comprises two mandatory components: (1) an artefact (Python code implementation) and (2) a written report, collectively accounting for 100% of the final mark.
1.
Introduction Understanding customer purchasing behaviour and product performance is crucial for organisations aiming to optimise sales strategies, improve customer engagement, and enhance profitability.
Businesses rely on data-driven insights to make informed decisions about product offerings, pricing, marketing, and customer retention.
Analysing sales transactions at the customer level enables businesses to identify high-value segments, track purchasing patterns, and assess the effectiveness of sales interventions.
In this context, a comprehensive sales dataset can support strategic decisions across departments, including marketing, operations, and finance.
2.

Dataset Information The Prodcut_Sales.csv dataset provides a detailed snapshot of product sales at the customer level.
It includes records of individual transactions, capturing key attributes such as customer ID, product ID, quantity sold, unit price, date of purchase, and product category.
The dataset also includes customer-specific features that can support segmentation and targeted analysis.
This data enables detailed exploration of customer-product interactions and supports use cases such as market basket analysis, sales forecasting, and customer lifetime value estimation.
The metadata of the dataset is available on the Moodle page (Metadata_Prodcut_Sales.txt).
3.

Tasks 3.1 Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) (20 Marks) • Clean and preprocess the dataset by handling missing values and outliers • Perform statistical analysis to understand data distribution • Document all data cleaning steps and transformations 3.2 Research Questions and Integration of Domain Knowledge (30 Marks) • Formulate three specific research questions based on the dataset • Integrate domain-specific knowledge to formulate your questions • Ensure questions are answerable with available data • Justify the relevance and importance of each question 3.3 Data Visualisation (40 Marks) • Create appropriate visualisations relevant to previous tasks and research questions • Apply appropriate colour schemes, visual encoding, labels, and legends • Optimise visualisations for clarity, impact taking into account your potential audience 3.4 Report Compilation (10 Marks) Compile a 4,000-word report (excluding references and appendices) using the provided template on Moodle (Report Submission Template) that synthesises all aspects of your analysis and visualisations into a cohesive narrative.

The report should cover: • Detailed interpretation of each visualisation • Identify key patterns, trends, and relationships • Support findings with statistical evidence • Draw meaningful conclusions from the visualisations • Address potential limitations and biases • Structure report with clear sections and flow • Include proper citations following the IEEE format • Create an engaging narrative connecting visualisations • Provide a summary of findings and limitations 4.

Overview You will build a small application using Java.
The coursework should be delivered in 3 sprints.
In each sprint, you will add new functionality and improve your code using the knowledge you will gain as the module progresses.
Planning and documentation are as important as working code.
We are looking for a professional approach that considers readability, maintainability, conformance to standards, and correct operation.
You will supply detailed documentation as well as code.
Please note that this is an individual piece of work.
You will be asked to present your work in person to a lecturer and answer questions about your solution.
You will have one practice assessment of sprint 1 (this won’t be graded – it’s just to help you check your progress) and two graded assessments.
Sprint 2 will be marked in code reviews in class.
You can only be marked for your sprint 2 if you have attended in-class assessment of sprint 1.

Task Please choose one of the following projects to develop in your coursework.
You should choose one project and stick to it throughout the module, fulfilling each of the sprint requirements in the context of your chosen project.
Think carefully about which topic interests you most, as you will work on it throughout the term.
Your overall aim is to produce well-architected OOP code that shows an understanding of the problem domain, created using standard OOP techniques, and properly documented both within the code and in accompanying design documents.
For each sprint, there will be well-defined basic requirements that must be met to achieve a pass, and advanced features that you can implement if you are aiming for higher marks.
We expect your code to conform to established coding standards as detailed here: https://google.github.io/styleguide/javaguide.html Projects SpareB&B Users can book different kinds of accommodation.

You can make any kind of accommodation available, for example, flats, hotels, luxury villas, or sofas.
Your accommodations may have different facilities, such as kitchens or washing machines.
ZipAbout Users can rent shared lightweight electric transport vehicles – bikes, scooters, skateboards, segway’s and other vehicles, perhaps yet to be invented.
For some vehicles, users will need equipment such as helmets, kneepads, or gloves to use them.
LibraryOfStuff Users can borrow all kinds of items - tools, sewing machines, phone chargers, bicycle pumps – little things we often need but can’t lay our hands on.
Items can be categorized by the part of the home in which they are usually used: kitchen, garden, workshop, or ‘out and about’.
Sprint 1 – Basic Classes - FORMATIVE assessment in lab sessions: Submission deadline: 24-October-2025  Consider the objects that can be booked, rented, or borrowed in your application.
Identify their methods and properties.

Use the OOP principles of Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, and Polymorphism to design your classes Create a class diagram showing the relationships between your classes.
Write well-documented Java code to implement your classes.
Minimum requirements should be: a constructor some properties a print () method which gives some user-friendly output.
Provide a Main class and main method that you can run in the console, in which: At least 3 objects of different types are created in your code A user-friendly listing of the objects can be printed to the console For those aiming for higher marks, also consider the additional information, e.g., facilities, equipment, and hobbies.
Consider how composition can be used to model these in your system.
Add them to your class diagram and code.
If you are seeking comprehensive feedback on your project activities, then please submit sprint 1 no later than 27-October-2025.

Please hand in your work in Moodle and seek feedback during the week 5 and 6 lab sessions.
Sprint 2:  Booking functionality    Submission Deadline: 21-November-2025 50% of marks  Implement a booking system for your chosen project in Java.
You do not need to implement booking for specific dates or durations, but it should be possible for a user to book and release items.
Once an item is booked, it should not be available for booking by any other user.
NOTE:  You do not have to capture any user input at this stage of development.
Basic requirements Provide a set of user stories to cover your provided functionality Provide a class diagram showing the relevant classes and relationships.
Your design and code should incorporate the sprint 1 requirements above, plus basic booking functionality.
Each class containing at least 3 properties/attributes and 3 methods.
Provide a Main class/method in which at minimum: At least 3 objects of different types are created directly in your code.

At least 3 users are created directly in your code.
In code, show that a booking can be made of an item by a user.
Show in your code that if another user tries to book the same item, they are politely informed that the item is unavailable.
User-friendly output can be printed showing correct information about items and the booking status at any particular time.
Advanced requirements  Basic requirements plus...
Your design incorporates the additional information, e.g., Facilities, equipment, and hobbies for bookable items Include at least one design pattern, accompanied by a short explanation of how it has been implemented, and/or Devise a feature of your own choice that demonstrates your deeper understanding of design patterns.
Perhaps by rewarding your application users in some way with loyalty points or a random prize draw, or perhaps by adding features to your application, such as managing cleaning or maintenance, or providing output in different formats (these are just examples).

Sprint 3 - GUI development   Submission Deadline: 7-January 2026 50% of marks Assessment based on demo and viva will be held in week 13.
Create and document a GUI for your application using JavaFX.
Basic requirements Documentation  Provide a schematic ‘wireframe’ that provides the specification for your GUI Provide a set of user stories and class diagrams that document the provided functionality.
Provide screenshots of your finished application.
Write a conclusion to your documentation in which you identify the programming paradigms that you have used to create your application, e.g., object-oriented, declarative, functional, and describe why each is suitable for different tasks.
Code  Implement basic button and list functionalities taught in class with some original design and formatting.
Use the classes you have created in sprint 2 to create some basic functionality where you list bookable items.

Advanced requirements  Use the classes you have created in sprint 2, including your design patterns, to implement the listing and selection of items, and provide feedback to the user.
You may implement additional features of your choice.
Use Java streams to implement at least one part of your application Ensure that these additional requirements are covered in your documentation.

How to Achieve Maximum Success To perform strongly in this assessment, go beyond simply meeting the minimum requirements of each sprint.
Focus on: Quality of Code Follow Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) principles (abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism) consistently.
Apply coding standards (Google Java Style Guide) to improve readability, maintainability, and professional presentation.
Use composition and association appropriately in your class design where relationships exist beyond inheritance.
Advanced Features For higher marks, integrate design patterns (e.g., Singleton, Observer, Factory) and explain their relevance.
Add value-added functionality such as loyalty schemes, maintenance tracking, or different output formats.
Leverage Java Streams or functional programming where relevant, especially in Sprint 3.
Documentation & Presentation Provide detailed class diagrams, user stories, and wireframes that accurately reflect your implementation.

Write clear, professional documentation explaining your design decisions and how they enhance usability and maintainability.
